title: SEQUIN: An imaging and analysis platform for quantification and characterization of synaptic structures in mouse
protocol: Rinse sections three times in 1× PBS to remove cryoprotectant.
Fill 6 well plate with PBS (∼12 mL/well) and add netwell inserts.
Fill 1 L beaker with distilled water.
Using a clean paintbrush, carefully move sections to netwells.
Ensure sections are fully submerged.
Rinse on shaker at low speed for 5 min.
Fill another 6 well plate with PBS and move netwells from first plate to second.
Rinse on shaker at low speed for 5 min.
Repeat steps 1e and 1f for 3 washes total.
Add blocking buffer to wells of a separate plate: ∼500 μL/well for a 24 well plate (up to 4 sections/well).
∼750 μL/well for a 12 well plate (up to 8 sections/well).
Carefully move sections from netwells with PBS to plates with blocking buffer using a clean paintbrush.
Cover and incubate at 20°C–24°C on shaker at low speed for 1 h.
Prepare primary antibody solutions while sections are incubating in blocking buffer.
Allow ∼500 μL/well for a 24 well plate (up to 4 sections/well) or ∼750 μL/well for a 12 well plate (up to 8 sections/well).
Prepare appropriate volumes of antibody “master mixes” as separate, 2× working solutions in antibody buffer.
When mixed 1:1 with a master mix of the other primary antibody or with an equivalent volume of antibody buffer, the final concentration is 1×.
Mix well for each antibody solution.
Centrifuge mixture at 10,000–17,000 × g for 5 min.
Avoid pellet when pipetting antibody.
Combine master mixes at a 1:1 ratio of anti-PSD-95 master mix to anti-synapsin master mix to create the final experimental solution.
Mix anti-PSD-95 master mix with antibody buffer at a 1:1 ratio to create the channel alignment control solution.
Mix either anti-PSD-95 or anti-synapsin master mix with antibody buffer at a 1:1 ratio to create the no-primary control solution.
Incubate sections in the prepared antibody labeling solutions for 16–24 hours at 20°C–24°C on a shaker.
Transfer tissue from the blocking buffer plate to the primary antibody plate using a paintbrush, ensuring sections are submerged and mobile.
Fill empty wells with distilled water and cover them.
Incubate the filled wells with sections in them for 16–24 hours at 20°C–24°C on a shaker at low speed.
Rinse sections three times for 5 minutes each in 1× PBS to remove unbound primary antibody.
Prepare fresh antibody buffer according to the specified protocol.
Add appropriate volumes of antibodies to the prepared antibody buffer and mix well.
Centrifuge the mixture at 10,000–17,000 × g for 5 minutes.
Avoid pellet when pipetting the antibody.
Incubate sections in secondary antibody solution while protecting from prolonged or bright illumination.
Plate the secondary antibodies.
Transfer tissue from PBS to secondary antibody.
Ensure sections are submerged and able to move freely.
Incubate on shaker at slow speed for 4 h at 20°C–24°C.
Prepare mounting media.
Calculate total volume required (150 μL/slide).
Mix AF300 and MWL-488 in a 1:9 ratio.
Vortex well.
Centrifuge until bubbles are gone.
Clean 1.5H coverslips with distilled water, then 100% ethanol.
Allow to dry in a warmer at 60°C.
Rinse sections three times in 1× PBS.
Mount tissue and coverslip in 1× PBS.
Dunk slide in distilled water 5 times quickly to remove salt residue.
Apply 150 μL mountant per slide by distributing among each section on the slide.
Slowly apply coverslip to avoid bubbles.
Store in dark, flat place at 20°C–24°C (room temperature) for mountant to cure.
Allow at least 3 and ideally 7 days after coverslipping for refractive index to plateau as mountant cures.
Apply Zeiss 518F immersion oil to objective.
Configure software in Zen Black by clicking “start system.”
Clean the slide using distilled water and lens cleaner while software loads.
Insert slide into Z-Piezo and tighten knobs until finger-tight for secure immobilization.
Navigate to “Maintain” tab within software.
Confirm objective listed in software matches that shown on freestanding microscope control box.
Ensure “Extended Z-Piezo” is unchecked under the “Hardware” tab settings.
Check “Adjust in continuous scans” and “Weak or sparse samples,” while unchecking “Adjust in slow time series.”
Set experimental parameters by moving to “Acquisitions” tab.
Choose “8-bit” bit depth for image acquisition.
Select “bidirectional” scan mode within software.
Use a zoom of at least 1.8× to facilitate post-acquisition Airyscan processing.
Choose “Line” scan mode in the settings.
Design appropriate light paths to image fluorophores being used, selecting 488 nm and 561 nm laser lines for fluorophores applied.
Open pinhole to its maximum size for imaging.
Set gain to 800 for optimal signal detection.
Configure the light path using the 488/561 main beam splitter.
Set the secondary beam splitter to “Plate.”
Select the emission filter as “BP 420–480 + BP 495–620.”
Click “Optimal” to set XY pixel resolution for all channels selected.
Navigate to region of interest (ROI) using epifluorescence light source and oculars.
Enable “Z-stack” in the top left corner of the “Acquisitions” tab.
In the “Z-stack” window, check “Use Piezo.”
Set Z-stack configuration to “First-Last” mode.
Select one laser channel and click “Live” in the top left panel of the “Acquisitions” tab.
Find the cut edge of the tissue at the cover glass using the Z-Piezo control knob.
Best fit display parameters to visualize signal if necessary.
Choose the most superficial Z position that avoids irregularity at the cut surface as “set first.”
Rotate the piezo focus control to find the deepest tissue section avoiding surface irregularity and select “set last.”
Navigate to the center of the stack by clicking “c” on the Z-stack diagram in the “Z-stack” window.
Set the step size (“Interval”) to 120 nm in the Z-stack window.
Set the number of optical sections (“Slices”) to 35 in the Z-stack window.
Scroll through the entirety of the stack and ensure qualitative suitability of all optical sections.
Turn off “Live” mode.
Align Airyscan detector.
Turn on “Continuous mode.”
Open the Airyscan view on the display window.
Wait until the brightest detector is centered before proceeding.
Set up laser ramping.
Check the “Z-correction” box in the Z-stack window.
Select the first channel to laser ramp for and start “Continuous” mode.
Move to the deepest position of the Z-stack.
Change the laser intensity of the selected channel until the lower 1/3 of the dynamic range is occupied, as represented by the histogram.
Move to the first position in the Z-stack.
Find the laser intensity that best replicates the signal acquired at the deepest position.
Repeat this process for all channels.
Set the desired laser ramp for all channels.
Return to the most superficial position.
Select all channels and enter the laser intensity for the first position for each channel.
Click “Add position” in the Z-stack window.
Move to the last position and repeat the previous steps.
Ensure acquisition speed is set to maximum.
Select “begin experiment” to start the scan.
Save the image upon completion of the scan.
Airyscan process the image.
Check the orthogonal view to ensure consistent Z intensity.
If brightness is not consistent, move to a different field and reset the laser ramp.
Select “Processing” tab within Zen Black and choose “Airyscan Process” from dropdown menu.
With the image of interest open, choose “Select Image.”
Set Airyscan strength to 6.
Choose “3D” option.
Click “Apply.”
Save new image as CZI.
Open previously acquired and Airyscan Processed channel alignment image and choose “Select Image” in the left sidebar.
Unselect “Fit.”
Offset one channel in Y such that channels are no longer overlapping to facilitate visualization of chromatic aberration.
Click “Apply” to create a new image.
View the orthogonal projection of this image and focus on one dual-labeled punctum.
Manually shift the Z value for one of the channels until the channel images are fully aligned.
Record the Z value offset.
Confirm suitability of adjustment value on multiple puncta throughout the image.
Open Imaris.
Place all Airyscan processed and channel-aligned images in a single folder.
Select images in Imaris (below steps describe spot creation using Imaris v9.5, but other versions are suitable with minor adaptations).
Choose “Channel Alignment” in the “Processing” tab.
Unselect “Fit.”
Input the recorded Z offset.
Save the new CZI file.
Optional: Click “Run Batch” to batch process files, ensuring “Auto” is unselected, strength set to 6.0, and “3D” selected.
Click “Observe Folder” and navigate to folder of CZI images.
Choose “Select Folder;” folder will be added to list of “Observed Folders.”
Open folder in Imaris (double-click).
Select all images in the folder, right click, and select “convert to IMS.”
Select “New Batch” in top menu.
When a preview of the image appears, select “Next” to begin object creation.
Click “Spots” button.
Create spots for each channel for analysis.
Set parameters for channel, size, and boundaries of spot creation in the “Create” window.
Check “Model PSF-elongation” along Z-axis and “Background Subtraction.”
“Estimated XY Diameter” for punctum is generally set to 0.2 μm.
Indicated X,Y, and Z puncta dimensions are appropriate for the indicated imaging parameters including the 63× 1.4 NA objective.
Navigate to the next screen.
Perform edge filtering to exclude spots not entirely contained within image boundaries.
Create two filters by clicking the plus sign twice.
Highlight one filter and change it to “Distance to Image Border XY Img=1” above automatic threshold.
Set the leftmost value of this filter to 0.1 μm and ensure rightmost value is not activated.
Change the second filter to “Position Z.”
Set the left and right values so they are 0.3 μm from the extremes for each image range.
Click the green arrow to complete the setup process for this analysis.
Repeat step for all channels in need of puncta detection.
Choose the “OK” button in the Objects window.
Name the batch.
Right click the new batch and select “Run Batch” to run on all images in the folder.
Export the results in the CSV file format.
Confirm identity of spots in output folders.
Check the batch name listed in column H of any CSV files output by Imaris.
Verify datasets based on the alphabetical order of user-defined spot names assigned in step 28.
Measure Euclidian distances between centroids of pre- and postsynaptic puncta using MATLAB for each punctum in 3 dimensions.
Sort separation data by distance to yield raw and binned data.
Use one marker as the reference dataset, typically PSD-95.
Match the nearest neighbor from the other dataset to each puncta in the referenced set.
Specify parameters for SEQUINv3.m analysis using Analysis parameters.txt file.
Run SEQUINv3.m with specified parameters.
Compile data using compileExceldocs_SEQUINv3.m.
Specify parameters for compileExceldocs_SEQUINv3.m using Compile Excel Docs parameters.txt file.
Open MATLAB.
Navigate to the folder containing the SEQUINv3 code in the MATLAB “Current Folder” window.
Edit the “Analysis parameters.txt” file to reflect all needed parameters.
Paste all the text of the user-updated “Analysis parameter.txt” file into MATLAB’s command window and press “enter.”
Compile Pre-to-Postsynaptic Puncta Separation Analysis data into one workbook.
Navigate to the folder containing the compileExceldocs_SEQUINv3.m code in MATLAB’s “Current Folder” window.
Edit the “Compile Excel Docs parameters.txt” file to reflect all needed parameters.
Paste all the text of the user-updated “Compile Excel Docs parameters.txt” file into MATLAB’s command window and press “enter.”
Call the compileExceldocs_SEQUINv3 script to compile all Pre-to-Postsynaptic Puncta Separation Analysis outputs into a single file in the newly created “compileddata” folder.
Retrieve generated pre-to-postsynaptic separation distances from the “data output” folder where the input Imaris data was located.
Open the tab “Normal Frequency” within the Excel doc to view frequency distributions of images sorted into bins of 20 nm.
Graph data.
Plot the frequency distribution data from the “Normal Frequency” tab in Excel.
Use a geometric series “10 nm, 30 nm, 50 nm, […]” as the center of histogram bins.
Model all graphs and subsequent quantifications using GraphPad Prism.
Any statistical software package can be used for modeling.
